name: Skullpill

lead: The skullpill is a framework in looksmaxxing communities holding that the underlying skull, meaning its length, width, height and the relationship between braincase and face, largely determines how attractive a face looks. People use it to read their own proportions, identify which parts of their appearance are skeletal and which are soft tissue, skin or hair, and decide where to put effort.

The vocabulary comes from physical anthropology. The cephalic index compares head width with head length, and the facial index compares face height with face width. Forum threads poll members on which combinations look best and share annotated skull diagrams. Published research on skull indices exists for anthropology and medicine, but it has not tested these ratios as predictors of attractiveness.

paras: In practice the skullpill is a way of looking at yourself and others rather than a routine. Members compare photos from the front, side and top, estimate where they fall on the cephalic and facial index categories, and discuss which features are fixed bone and which can be changed through grooming, hairstyle, body fat, skin or surgery. Hairstyles that add or hide length and width, such as shorter sides or more volume on top, are a common practical takeaway.

The idea itself carries no physical risk, but forum discussion can be discouraging for people who conclude their skull shape is a fixed limit. Cephalic-index categories have a history in 19th and early 20th century racial anthropology, and anthropologists note the index cannot reliably identify an individual's ancestry. Surgical skull or jaw procedures discussed alongside the theory carry the usual operative risks.

lead: The skullpill is a framework in looksmaxxing and blackpill communities holding that the size and shape of the skull provide the underlying structure for facial attractiveness. Followers use it to read their own proportions, to separate features set by bone from those that can be changed through hair, grooming, body fat, skin or procedures, and to decide where to put effort.[1][2]

The vocabulary is borrowed from physical anthropology. The cephalic index, defined by the Swedish anatomist Anders Retzius (1796-1860), is maximum head width divided by maximum head length, multiplied by 100, and sorts heads into long and narrow (dolichocephalic), average (mesocephalic) and short and wide (brachycephalic) categories.[3][4] The facial index compares face height with face width, with terms such as leptoprosopic (long, narrow face) and euryprosopic (short, broad face).[5] Forum members poll one another on which combinations look best.[5]

Published work on the cephalic index concerns anthropology, medicine and forensics, and a recent systematic review describes it as useful for average head shape in populations but unable to determine an individual's ancestry.[3] Separate research on facial attractiveness has examined averageness, symmetry, sexual dimorphism and facial proportions, but the studies located for this article do not rate attractiveness by cephalic-index category.[6]
infobox: Skull shape sets a ceiling on facial attractiveness[1]

paras: Followers describe the skull as the foundation under skin and fat. Threads such as "Understanding the Skull Pill" lay out basic dimensions (length, width, height) and note that indices are ratios, so a head can be called long or narrow relative to its own proportions rather than in absolute size.[2] The same thread notes that a tall skull can be brachycephalic and a vertically short one dolichocephalic, though other members say such combinations are rare and that broad-headed people tend to have shorter faces.[2]

Another long-running thread frames the skull as the central factor, with its author stating that he can rate people from behind and that "skull is everything", while asking what objectively makes skulls look striking, such as the ratio of braincase to face.[1] Replies in the same thread push back on the claim, showing that the community itself debates it.[1]

sections.h: How people use it to look better
paras: In practice the skullpill is a way of looking at oneself and others. Members compare photos from the front, side and top, estimate where they fall on the index categories, and discuss which features are fixed bone and which are soft tissue, skin or hair.[5][2]

The practical takeaways members describe are mostly about the changeable layer: hairstyles that add or hide length and width, body-fat level, skin and eyewear, with surgery discussed for what bone allows.[1][2] One thread titled "the skullpill is avoidable" argues the limit can be worked around, though its post text is not reproduced here.[7]

The cephalic index is calculated on the living head or the skull. Wikipedia lists bands from below 65.5 (ultradolichocephalic) through 75.0-79.9 (mesocephalic) to 80.0-84.9 (brachycephalic) and 90 or above (ultrabrachycephalic), and notes that living-head values include scalp tissue and are not directly comparable with dry-skull values.[3] Measurement has moved from calipers to cephalometric radiography, CT and 3D modelling.[3]

Population values form a continuous spectrum rather than separate types; in one Delhi autopsy series cited by Wikipedia, about 81% of individuals fell between 72.5 and 84.9.[3] The facial index is a separate ratio taken in front view, and a forum megapoll lists combinations such as brachy-euryprosopic or brachy-leptoprosopic with example index values (for instance 0.825 against 0.925) and asks which is best for men.[5] The poll is opinion among site members and not a published study.[5]

Anders Retzius was professor of anatomy at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm; his studies of the human cranium produced the dolichocephalic and brachycephalic classifications.[4][3] The index was first used in physical anthropology to classify ancient human remains from Europe.[3]

The forum framework itself is a later, informal development. The looksmax.org threads cited here were started by members and are undated in the pages consulted, and the term skullpill sits alongside other bone-structure frameworks in the community's vocabulary.[1][2]

Nineteenth and early twentieth century racial anthropology used cranial indices to model population movements. Wikipedia reports that Carleton Coon was still using the index in the 1960s, by which time it was largely discredited as a racial classifier.[3] Franz Boas's 1910-1912 study of immigrants' children suggested head form responds to environment; Sparks and Jantz (2002) reanalysed the data and reported a relatively high genetic component, while Gravlee and colleagues (2003) concluded most of Boas's findings held.[3] Retzius's polygenist views and association with phrenology led the Swedish Society for Anthropology and Geography in 2015 to decide against awarding a medal in his name.[4]

Modern uses are medical and population-level: assessing and planning correction of cranial deformity and checking fetal head shape on ultrasound, where about 78% is a typical value.[3] A 2026 systematic review of 31 studies found the index useful for average head shape, tracking generational change and setting local clinical reference values, but not for determining an individual's ancestry.[3] Population means have shifted over time; Korean data span about 2,000 years and show a move toward brachycephaly followed by a reversal in people born after the mid-1960s.[3]

Facial-attractiveness research examines other variables. Studies summarised on Wikipedia report preferences for averaged faces, facial symmetry and, in some samples, sexual dimorphism; an Italian study of 324 adolescents found that those selected as attractive tended to have a larger forehead-to-face ratio, wider-set eyes and reduced total facial height, which the authors read as neotenous features.[6] Other reports in the same article question how strongly masculinity predicts attractiveness once perceived health is accounted for.[6] None of this work sorts faces by cephalic-index category.

The idea itself carries no physical risk. Forum discussion can be discouraging for people who conclude their skull shape is a fixed limit, a pattern visible in members describing themselves in self-deprecating terms in the megapoll.[5] Cephalic-index categories carry a history in racial anthropology, and anthropologists state the index cannot reliably identify an individual's ancestry.[3] Surgical procedures discussed alongside the theory carry the usual operative risks.

No studies found. Research on the cephalic index is anthropological and clinical, and studies of facial attractiveness address averageness, symmetry and facial proportions rather than skull index categories.[3][6]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the skullpill is discussed as a diagnostic framework, with threads on index categories, skull diagrams and polls on preferred proportions.[5][2][1]

claims.claim: Skull shape caps how attractive a face can be
Certain cephalic and facial index combinations are most attractive in men
Broad skulls go with short faces and long skulls with long faces
The braincase-to-face ratio is a key determinant of skull appeal

timeline.event: Anders Retzius, later credited with defining the cephalic index, is born in Sweden.[4]
Retzius is elected to the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences.[4]
Franz Boas studies the head shape of immigrants' children, suggesting environmental influence on head form.[3]
Carleton Coon still uses the cephalic index, by which time it is described as largely discredited for race classification.[3]
Sparks and Jantz reanalyse Boas's data and report a relatively high genetic component.[3]
Gravlee, Bernard and Leonard reanalyse the data and conclude most of Boas's findings hold.[3]
The Swedish Society for Anthropology and Geography decides against a medal in Retzius's name.[4]
A systematic review of 31 studies (Nair et al.) assesses the cephalic index's population and clinical uses and its limits for individual ancestry.[3]
